title: CAP Theorem
lesson:
CAP theorem describes a hard tradeoff faced by any distributed data store: Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance can't all be fully guaranteed at once. Consistency here means linearizable consistency — every read sees the most recent successful write, or an error, never a stale value. Availability means every request to a non-failed node gets a non-error response, though not necessarily the latest data. Partition tolerance means the system keeps operating even when network messages between nodes are delayed or dropped, splitting the cluster into groups that can't talk to each other.

In practice, partition tolerance isn't optional for a genuinely distributed system — networks fail, packets get dropped, and a system spanning multiple machines or data centers will eventually see a partition whether it wants one or not. That means the real, actionable choice CAP forces is between consistency and availability during a partition. Systems that choose consistency (CP) will refuse to serve requests on the minority side of a partition rather than risk returning stale or conflicting data — ZooKeeper, etcd, and HBase behave this way. Systems that choose availability (AP) keep answering requests on both sides of the partition even though the two sides may now disagree — Cassandra and DynamoDB default to this, though both offer tunable consistency levels per request.

Concretely, a CP system under partition will reject writes (and often reads) on whichever side can't reach a quorum of nodes, trading availability for a guarantee that nothing inconsistent is ever returned. An AP system instead keeps both sides live, letting them accumulate diverging versions of the same records; once the partition heals, it must reconcile those divergent writes using techniques like vector clocks, last-write-wins timestamps, or CRDTs. Neither choice is universally correct — it depends on whether your application would rather show an error or show possibly-stale data.

It's also worth knowing CAP only describes behavior during an actual partition; the PACELC extension notes that even without a partition, distributed systems still trade latency for consistency (the "else, Latency vs Consistency" half of PACELC). And CAP's framing as a single global binary choice is a simplification — many real systems use quorum-based reads and writes (N replicas, W required for a write, R required for a read) that let each individual request tune its own point on the consistency/availability spectrum rather than locking the whole system into one mode.

questions.prompt: In CAP terms, what does "availability" specifically mean?
options: Every request receives a response containing the most recent write
Every request to a non-failed node receives a non-error response, though possibly stale
The system never needs to be taken down for maintenance
Reads are always served faster than writes
questions.explanation: CAP availability means non-failed nodes always answer with a non-error response; it says nothing about that response being the latest data.

questions.prompt: Cassandra and DynamoDB default to AP behavior, continuing to serve requests on both sides of a partition.
questions.explanation: Both default to availability during a partition, letting the sides diverge and reconciling later, though both also expose tunable per-request consistency levels.

questions.prompt: The extension of CAP noting that even with no partition a distributed system still trades latency against consistency is called ____.
questions.explanation: PACELC adds "else, Latency vs Consistency" to CAP's partition-time Consistency vs Availability choice.

questions.prompt: After an AP system heals from a partition, how does it handle records that diverged on each side?
options: It discards every write made during the partition
It merges the divergent versions using techniques like vector clocks, last-write-wins timestamps, or CRDTs
It blocks all reads until an administrator manually picks a winner
It switches permanently into CP mode to prevent it happening again
questions.explanation: An AP system reconciles conflicting versions after the partition heals using conflict-resolution mechanisms such as vector clocks, last-write-wins, or CRDTs.

questions.prompt: CAP forces a permanent, system-wide choice of two properties that can never be tuned on a per-request basis.
questions.explanation: CAP only constrains behavior during an actual partition; quorum-based N/W/R configuration lets individual requests pick their own point on the consistency/availability spectrum.

questions.prompt: Order these events from a CP system's perspective when a partition isolates a minority of its nodes, earliest first.
items: Requests on the minority side are rejected rather than risk returning inconsistent data
A partition separates the cluster into a majority side and a minority side
When the partition heals, the minority nodes rejoin and catch up from the majority
The minority side finds it cannot reach a quorum of nodes
questions.explanation: The partition happens, the minority side loses quorum, a CP system rejects requests there to stay consistent, and the minority catches up once the partition heals.
